opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the most useful things about a responsible scaling policy is that it lets people who disagree about how likely catastrophic risks are still agree on what to do about them.

If you talk to people across the field, you get a huge range of views. Some people think models capable of meaningfully helping with something like a bioweapons attack are a few years away. Others think it's decades off, or that the whole concern is overblown. If the conversation is "should we pause AI development now," you just get gridlock, because people are arguing about forecasts nobody can really verify.

An RSP reframes the question. It says: we're not going to argue about when a dangerous capability shows up. We're going to agree that *if* a model shows it, then we'll have these safeguards in place before we keep scaling or deploying. That conditional structure is what makes agreement possible. Someone who thinks the risk is far away can sign on, because to them the commitment costs almost nothing in the near term. Someone who thinks the risk is close is reassured, because there's a concrete tripwire that triggers real action instead of a vague promise to be careful.

So the hard work shifts to things that are more tractable. What evaluations tell us a model has crossed a threshold? What security and deployment protections are adequate at each level? Those are empirical and technical questions people can make progress on together, instead of a values-and-vibes debate about timelines.

There's also an accountability benefit. When the commitments are written down and public, outsiders can check whether a company is living up to them, other labs can adopt similar frameworks, and governments get a template for what reasonable regulation could look like. Ideally it becomes a shared standard rather than one company's internal policy.

It's not a perfect solution. The evaluations are still immature, and there's real pressure on any company to interpret its own thresholds generously. But as a way to get broad agreement on precautions before we're in the middle of a crisis, I think the "if-then" approach is one of the most promising tools we have.

r001.rationale: It separates forecasts about when dangerous capabilities will emerge from agreeing in advance on safeguards if a model demonstrates them.

r002.rationale: It says people with differing views—even those who consider the concern overblown—can agree to safeguards conditional on a model crossing an evaluated capability threshold.

r003.rationale: It ties safeguards to a capability tripwire, with protections triggered when a model demonstrates dangerous capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it is that there's a huge amount of disagreement right now about how dangerous AI is going to be and when. Some people think we're a few years away from systems that could cause catastrophic harm, and some people think that's decades away or basically never. And if you try to get those two groups to agree today on what precautions we should take, you're going to fail, because they're starting from completely different premises.

What a responsible scaling policy does is it sort of sidesteps that disagreement. Instead of saying "AI is dangerous, so we need to do X," it says "if a model has these specific capabilities, then we need these specific safeguards before we train or deploy it." And it turns out that's something people can agree on even if they disagree about the timelines. If you think dangerous capabilities are 20 years away, you can still agree that once a model can, say, meaningfully help someone make a bioweapon, you'd want strong security and misuse protections in place. You just think that trigger won't fire for a long time. And if you think it's two years away, you agree with the same conditional, you just expect it to fire soon.

So the commitment is conditional on evidence. You run evaluations, you check whether the model crosses certain thresholds, and the precautions kick in when it does. That lets you make decisions based on what you actually observe rather than on who had the better forecast in an argument.

The other thing I'd say is it makes the precautions concrete and testable. It's very easy to say "we take safety seriously." It's much harder to say "here's the specific threshold, here's the test, here's what we commit to doing if we cross it," and then have other people be able to look at that and critique it. That's where I think a lot of the value comes from. It gives everyone, inside the company and outside, something specific to push on, rather than a vague sense of whether a lab is being careful enough.

And honestly, it also helps internally. When you have a thousand people working at a company, you need some shared framework for making these calls, so it isn't just a handful of people's intuitions in the moment. Writing it down ahead of time, before you're under commercial pressure to ship something, means you're making the decision with clearer heads.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts arguing that AI is dangerous with setting safeguards that take effect when a model demonstrates specified capabilities, separating the danger assessment from the precaution decision.

r002.rationale: It says people with different timelines, including those who think catastrophic danger is decades away or never, can agree to the same precautions once evaluations show a model has dangerous capabilities.

r003.rationale: It states that safeguards kick in when evaluations show a model crossing capability thresholds, tying precautions to the point those capabilities create danger.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the disagreement about AI risk is about when we should expect particular capabilities to show up, and how dangerous those capabilities will be. You can have one person who thinks catastrophic risks are quite close and another who thinks they’re very far away, and it’s hard to get them to agree on precautions we should take today.

Responsible scaling policies let you ask a more conditional question: what would we need to see in a model to agree that additional precautions were warranted? If a model could help someone develop a biological weapon, for example, what safeguards should be in place before we deploy it? People can agree on that even if they disagree about whether we’ll reach that capability next year or in ten years.

That gives you a way to make progress without first resolving every disagreement about the future. You identify concerning capabilities, figure out how to test for them, and commit in advance to the protections you’ll need if they emerge. Of course, that only works if the tests are meaningful and the commitments actually constrain what the company does—including slowing down if it can’t put the necessary safeguards in place.

r001.rationale: It separates identifying a concerning capability from deciding what safeguards should be in place if that capability appears.

r002.rationale: It says people can agree despite disagreeing about when a dangerous capability will emerge, but does not cover disagreement about whether AI will ever pose catastrophic danger.

r003.rationale: It says to commit to protections if concerning capabilities emerge and have safeguards in place before deploying a model with them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the difficulty is that people disagree quite a lot about how quickly AI is going to become more capable, and when particular risks are going to emerge. If you try to get everyone to agree on a set of precautions we should take today, that disagreement can make it hard to get very far.

Responsible scaling policies let you make the agreement conditional. You can say, “If a model could help someone carry out a catastrophic biological attack, what safeguards should we have before we deploy it?” You don’t have to agree that the next model will be able to do that. You can disagree about whether that’s a year away or ten years away, while still agreeing that, if we see that capability, we should take certain precautions.

That also makes the discussion more concrete. What would we test for? What evidence would trigger stronger security or restrictions on deployment? And what would we do if we couldn’t put those safeguards in place? Ideally, you agree on those things in advance, rather than having the whole debate for the first time when you have a model you’re under pressure to release.

So I see them as a way to turn some of the disagreement about forecasts into agreement about how we should respond to evidence. Of course, that only helps if the evaluations are meaningful and the commitments actually constrain what the company does.

r001.rationale: The response separates agreement about whether a model will have a dangerous capability from agreement about precautions to take if that capability appears.

r002.rationale: It says people may disagree about when risks will emerge, but does not clearly say they can disagree about whether AI will ever pose catastrophic danger while still agreeing on precautions conditional on evaluations demonstrating that danger.

r003.rationale: It ties precautions to seeing dangerous capabilities in a model and to evidence that triggers safeguards, rather than to a fixed forecast.
